clue.text: An extraordinarily short book

indicators.note: short tells us to cut the last letter off the word just given

parts.note: extraordinarily means to the highest degree, most, as in 'most kind'

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a certain volume is remarkably brief.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims MOST to MOS. Amos really is a short book of the Old Testament, which makes the surface reading true as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Amos is one of the minor prophets of the Old Testament, whose writings form a biblical book.

clue.text: You'll see what teacher does with essay I wrote

definitions.text: what teacher does with essay I wrote

explanation.surface: A pupil warns that the teacher's marking of their essay will prove them right.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is read twice: as a warning that events will prove the speaker right, and literally as a teacher grading the words a pupil wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a prediction meaning 'you will find I was right'; literally, a teacher grades the writing a pupil hands in.

clue.text: Theologians make solemn move round church, and round

indicators.note: the first round tells us the shuffled letters go around the next pieces
move tells us to shift the letters of solemn into a new order

parts.note: a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Clergy are told to process solemnly around a church and then circle it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' signals the anagram and the first 'round' the container; the second 'round' is the circle letter. Schoolmen were the scholastic teachers of medieval universities.
explanation.definitionFit: Medieval scholastic theologians teaching in the universities were known as schoolmen.

clue.text: Dicey business, finding two sorts of bacon

parts.note: back is a lean British cut of bacon from the loin
gammon is cured ham from the hind leg of a pig, a British bacon cut

explanation.surface: A risky venture turns out to involve two kinds of cured pork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicey' is literal: the game is played with dice. BACK and GAMMON are both British names for kinds of bacon.
explanation.definitionFit: A board game in which counters move according to throws of dice, so it is literally a business with dice.

clue.text: Shattered, each imbibing hot African drink

indicators.note: imbibing means taking in, so the hot letter goes inside

parts.note: shattered means broken, which is bust
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps
EA is the usual abbreviation for each, as on price tags

explanation.surface: Someone exhausted downs a hot drink from Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shattered' and 'imbibing' suggest a tired drinker, but 'imbibing' is the container signal, slotting the hot letter in after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: A herbal infusion brewed in southern Africa from wild shrubs, such as rooibos or honeybush.

clue.text: Miss it and crashland at sea?

definitions.text: Miss it and crashland at sea?

indicators.note: at sea means confused and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written as part of the letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: A pilot fears missing the tiny target and ditching into the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at sea' signals the anagram; the 'and' between the two fodder pieces is a link. The whole clue also describes the danger of overshooting a small island in the Indian Ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: A small remote Australian territory in the Indian Ocean, easy for a pilot to overshoot and end up in the water.

clue.text: Trader offers short book — good? Not very, when picked up

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards
Not says the very letter is to be left out of the book

parts.note: a novella is a short novel

explanation.surface: A dealer offers a slim volume, asks whether it's good, and admits it isn't.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not' removes V from NOVELLA to leave NOELLA; add G and 'when picked up' turns NOELLAG to read upward. 'short book' tempts with GAL for Galatians, a dead end.
explanation.definitionFit: A large sailing ship of the 16th and 17th centuries used by Spain for trade with its colonies.

clue.text: Mount to speak for head of corporation

indicators.note: to speak means the horse word is said out loud and heard as another

parts.note: a mount is a horse for riding, such as a mare

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to climb up and address the boss of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: In British non-rhotic speech MARE and the civic leader sound identical. 'corporation' here is a town council, not a company.
explanation.definitionFit: A municipal corporation is a town council, and its elected chief is the civic leader with a chain of office.

clue.text: Time to pray? Nothing to say at first

parts.note: none means nothing, not any

indicators.note: at first takes only the opening letter of the word say

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is prayer time and finds they have nothing to say.
explanation.walkthrough: Monastic offices fall at set hours of the day; this one is the ninth hour, mid-afternoon.
explanation.definitionFit: In the monastic day the office of prayer said at the ninth hour, about 3 p.m., is one of the canonical hours.

clue.text: Such music, golden bird being in earshot

parts.note: or is the heraldic word for gold

indicators.note: in earshot means heard, so the bird's name is taken by its sound

parts.note: a kestrel is a small falcon

explanation.surface: A piece of music is likened to a golden bird singing nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such' makes the definition 'music of this kind'. OR is heraldic gold; the bird of prey's name heard aloud gives the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Music scored for a full symphonic ensemble of strings, wind and percussion is described this way.

clue.text: Colour unknown in tin

indicators.note: in places the unknown letter inside the tin

parts.note: a tin is a can, a metal container
Y is a mathematical unknown, like x and z

explanation.surface: A paint colour remains a mystery inside its tin.
explanation.definitionFit: A greenish-blue shade, one of the primary inks used in colour printing.

clue.text: Majority accepting penny on one tax

indicators.note: on means the majority-and-penny piece is placed after the one

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: accepting means taking in, so the penny goes inside

parts.note: the majority is most of something

explanation.surface: Most people accept a penny charge on each item.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepting' puts P inside MOST, and 'on' places that after I in this across clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A levy or duty imposed by authority, especially a customs charge on imported goods.

clue.text: Officials in groups proceed to return

indicators.note: return tells us the whole combination is read backwards
in puts the proceed word inside the groups word

parts.note: sets are groups of things
to draw is to move or proceed, as in draw near

explanation.surface: Officials move in groups and go back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is the container signal and 'to return' reverses the whole result, not just the second word.
explanation.definitionFit: Officials who manage a race meeting or public event are known by this title.

clue.text: A thunder god's terrible craft

indicators.note: terrible means awful, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written as part of the letters to shuffle
the possessive god's gives the word god

explanation.surface: Thor's fearsome vessel is described.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' shuffles ATHUNDERGOD. 'craft' is a vessel, not a skill.
explanation.definitionFit: A type of big-gun battleship named after HMS Dreadnought of 1906, a fearsome naval vessel.

clue.text: Total secured with having pooled one's efforts?

indicators.note: secured means held in, so the with letter is enclosed

parts.note: a total is a sum

explanation.surface: A team got the full amount by pulling together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pooled one's efforts' normally means cooperated; here it means made one's efforts in a pool. 'having' marks the past participle.
explanation.definitionFit: The past participle of the verb for moving through water, as in a swimming pool.

clue.text: Tread clumsily holding skirts, wanting to run

indicators.note: holding means containing, so the skirts go inside
clumsily means awkwardly, so the letters of tread are rearranged

parts.note: minis are miniskirts

explanation.surface: Someone stumbles about in short skirts, longing to dash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clumsily' signals the anagram and 'holding' the container. 'run' is to manage, not to dash; 'wanting to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To manage or direct the affairs of an organisation, as one runs a business.

clue.text: It's threatening a hummingbird

parts.note: the 's of it's stands for is, contributing just the letter S
a-brewing is an old-fashioned way of saying about to break, as a storm is

explanation.surface: Something menacing turns out to be a tiny bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's threatening' is read as the folksy phrase "'s a-brewing", as in 'there's a storm a-brewing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A family of large tropical American hummingbirds named for the curved, blade-like shafts of their wing feathers.

clue.text: Given new pitch, son departs to play

indicators.note: to play means to move about freely, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written as part of the letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: A son leaves to perform after the music has been put into a different key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to play' shuffles SONDEPARTS. 'pitch' is musical key, not a sports field.
explanation.definitionFit: Music rewritten or performed in a different key has been shifted in pitch.

clue.text: Very keen to stay over in conference centre

indicators.note: over in a down clue means the run is turned upside down, read from the bottom

parts.note: mad means wildly enthusiastic, as in mad about
to stop is to stay somewhere, as in stopping overnight

explanation.surface: Eager delegates want to stay over at a conference venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns MADSTOP to read upward. 'over' looks like part of 'stay over' but is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A German city near Berlin that hosted the 1945 Allied summit deciding post-war Germany's fate.

clue.text: Sound measure of the French bubbly, initially chilled, served up

indicators.note: this word means the letters it governs are turned round, so they are read backwards

parts.note: le is French for the

indicators.note: initially takes only the first letter of bubbly

parts.note: chilled means cooled, iced

explanation.surface: Champagne is served cold, French style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served up' turns LEBICED to read upward in this down clue. 'bubbly' and 'chilled' paint champagne, but give one letter and a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A logarithmic unit for loudness, a tenth of a bel, used to measure noise.

clue.text: With daring dropping all learners in group

indicators.note: dropping means losing, so letters are taken out

parts.note: to act with daring is to act boldly
L is the learner-driver plate letter, and all learners means both Ls

explanation.surface: A team takes a risk by dropping all its trainees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping' removes both Ls from BOLDLY, as 'all' learners means every L in the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of people is an organised group, such as a governing body.

clue.text: Criminal set restrained by orders we now know to be dangerous

definitions.text: we now know to be dangerous

indicators.note: restrained by means held inside, so the shuffled letters go into the orders

parts.note: ASBOs are British anti-social behaviour orders, court orders restraining troublemakers

indicators.note: criminal means wrong or crooked, so the letters of set are rearranged

explanation.surface: A criminal gang is curbed by court orders imposed on dangerous offenders.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' signals the anagram and 'restrained by' the container. ASBOs were British court orders against nuisance behaviour, a familiar crossword source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous mineral once widely used for insulation, later found to cause lung disease and cancer.

clue.text: Head of army, say, is offering protection

indicators.note: head of takes the first letter of army

parts.note: say means for example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: A general's job, say, is to provide protection.
explanation.definitionFit: Under someone's sponsorship or shelter, from the shield of Zeus in Greek myth.

clue.text: Suddenly appear in profit, in old money?

parts.note: a bob was a shilling in pre-decimal British currency
being up means ahead on one's money, in profit

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a sudden gain would be counted in pre-decimal coins.
explanation.walkthrough: A bob was a British shilling, five pence after 1971; being a bob up was being a shilling ahead.
explanation.definitionFit: To pop up into view unexpectedly, like a float rising to the surface.

clue.text: Musical movements insufficiently rhythmic — redo some

indicators.note: insufficiently means the words are not used in full, only a stretch of letters inside them

explanation.surface: A conductor tells players their rhythm isn't good enough and some parts must be done again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'insufficiently' points to a part of the following words: the run of letters ending 'rhythmic', the whole of 'redo' and the start of 'some'.
explanation.definitionFit: Settings of the Nicene creed are sections of a sung Mass, as in a Requiem or Missa.

clue.text: Taunt soldier, and live

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a soldier and stays alive.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeer or mocking remark, a sneering insult.

clue.text: One's down for admission to old castle

definitions.text: One's down for admission to old castle

parts.words: One's down for admission to old castle
parts.note: reads like a person's name being on a list for entry to a castle, but describes the bridge lowered to let visitors cross a moat

explanation.surface: Someone's name is on the list for entry to a historic fortress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'down' looks like a list entry; it is literal: the bridge is lowered to let people in.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle's hinged bridge across the moat, lowered to allow entry and raised for defence.

clue.text: Great way to put on pounds? She wouldn't

indicators.note: to put on means to add, so the pounds letter is attached after the way word

parts.note: super means great, excellent
a mode is a way or manner
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A great way to gain weight is offered, and a woman declines.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers back to the first sentence: a model on the catwalk would never put on pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A top fashion model is famously expected to stay thin, so she would never gain weight.

clue.text: Didn't buy anything? Come on!

parts.note: having bought nothing one got nothing, and got stands for the buying
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A shopper returns empty-handed and is urged to try again.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic exclamation 'go to!' meant 'come, come!' in Shakespeare's day. 'Didn't buy anything' is read as got zero.
explanation.definitionFit: An old exclamation of impatience or encouragement, found in Shakespeare and the Bible.
